title: the one behind your eyes
hookLine: a king's prize of a thousand cows, and a sage asked to point at the self
tomorrow: the ocean the wave forgets it is
last: DO THE THING THAT'S YOURS TO DO.

lines: A THOUSAND COWS, GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.
cards: King Janaka once held a great gathering of sages, and set out a thousand cows with gold tied to their horns, a prize for whoever knew the most about the highest truth. Nobody dared claim them.
Then the sage Yajnavalkya calmly told his student: drive them home. The other sages were furious, and one by one they stood up to test him.
One, a man named Ushasta, pressed him on a single point: show me this self you speak of. Plainly. The way you'd point and say: that's a cow, that's a horse.
Today's word is what he was asking to see.

teach.h: ATMAN — THE SELF THAT IS AWARE
teach.b: Atman. The self. Not the self in selfie, the personality you show the world.
The Upanishads use atman for the deepest you: the one that is aware. Yajnavalkya's answer turns Ushasta's question around: you can't see the seer of seeing. You can't hear the hearer of hearing.
The one who looks can't become one more thing on the table to be looked at.

teach.h: NETI, NETI — NOT THIS, NOT THIS
teach.b: Elsewhere the same Upanishad describes the self by saying what it is not: neti, neti. Not this, not this. Whatever you can point to, the body, the breath, the busy mind, the self is not that.
This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: you are not only your body, your moods or your story.
Hindu scripture teaches that the atman isn't born and doesn't die; bodies change around it, even life after life.
That's why, at a funeral, a Hindu family may say the one they loved hasn't simply ended: the body is set down, and the self goes on.
Hindu schools describe the atman in different ways. Some teach that the self is one with the whole. Others teach that it is a distinct soul, forever dear to God and dependent on God.
Tomorrow brings the word for the whole. And the turn is practical. When worry comes, it comes as something seen: a thought, a tight chest, a story about tomorrow.
The Upanishad points past all of it, to the one who sees, the part of you no bad day can touch.

how: Hindus who follow the Upanishads study the self through teachers and texts, and in meditation and self-inquiry turn attention from thoughts to the one who is aware of them; schools differ on how the self relates to God.

games.why: Yajnavalkya told Ushasta the self can't be pointed at, because it's the seer of seeing. Atman is the one who is aware, not a ghost and not the personality.

practice: Today's practice is to notice the noticer. Let your eyes close or soften. Let a thought arrive, any thought.
Don't follow it. Just see that it's there. Now notice that something saw it.
Rest there for a moment, not in the thought, in the seeing. Another thought will come; that's what thoughts do. Same move: see it, then notice the one who saw.
No need to get anywhere. The bell holds the time.

wordCard.voice: Atman. The self: not the body, not the thoughts, but the one aware of them. Tenth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the self, the inner one who is aware.

carryVoice: Your line: someone is in there. That's the atman. When worry shows up today, ask once, quietly: who is seeing this? Day ten.
